newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-HEADINGLEY OWNERS URGE YORKSHIRE TO STAY.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-HEADINGLEY OWNERS URGE YORKSHIRE TO STAY.

text.p: The owners of Headingley, one of England's best known cricket grounds, tried on Tuesday to persuade Yorkshire not to leave for a new 50-million-pounds ($78 million) stadium near Wakefield.

Yorkshire said at a press conference on Monday they would abandon the Leeds ground before the end of the century, ending more than 100 years' association between club and site and threatening Headingley's status as a test match venue.
The county side are tenants at the historic ground and say they are frustrated over their inability to capitalise fully on test match proceeds or to expand the limited facilities.
The new 25,000-capacity all-seater stadium they plan to move to is to be built at nearby Wakefield and will include five practice pitches, a cricket academy, a museum, a hotel and a railway station.
But on Tuesday, Headingley's owners, the Leeds Cricket, Football and Athletic Company, said they would urge Yorkshire to change their minds.
"We were disappointed with the Yorkshire statement at their press conference of their intention to leave Headingley," the company said in a statement.
"We believe there is a long way to go before their move becomes a reality and we will continue in our attempts to convince them to remain at Headingley.
"We believe that we had an agreement that they would keep us informed of their intentions via our joint committee."
Headingley has been a test match venue since the end of the last century, when England and Australia met there in 1899 in the first test to be played there.
